replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text:
Thank you for raising this painful part of Tasmania’s history. The violence, dispossession, forced removals, and the 1830 “Black Line” against Aboriginal Tasmanians are very real and deserve to be remembered. The Black Line involved more than 2,000 settlers, soldiers, police, and convicts trying to drive Aboriginal people from their lands, and many survivors were later removed to Flinders Island.
One detail is worth clarifying, though: the claim that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were still legally treated as game with bounties on their heads until 1960 is not supported by the historical sources we checked. Also, Torres Strait Islander peoples are from the Torres Strait region, not Tasmania. Tasmanian Aboriginal people and their descendants survived, and their communities and culture continue today.
Thank you for bringing attention to this history. It is an important part of Tasmania’s story, and we should treat it with care and accuracy.

comments.author: @Bor.der.Collie
comments.text: A fascinating film about Tasmania—an island that, to a Central European, feels as remote as the moon. Some of its flora and fauna have remained unchanged for hundreds of thousands of years. But why do forest fires occur so frequently? In Europe, forests are often deliberately set ablaze to clear land, but surely the people of Tasmania are aware of the forest's importance? Personally, I would have liked to learn more about Tasmania's origins—specifically from a geological perspective—but the film was very interesting nonetheless.

replies.author: @Bor.der.Collie
replies.text: ​@HappyTravel99 thank you for your answer

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text:
Thank you for such a thoughtful comment. Tasmania’s bushfires are not simply a case of forests being deliberately cleared. Natural ignitions such as lightning can start fires, while accidental human causes, arson, and planned fuel-reduction burns also occur. Fire is actually a natural part of many Tasmanian ecosystems, although severe bushfires can still be extremely destructive.
And your point about geology is a very good one. Tasmania has an unusually rich geological history, with rocks spanning a huge portion of Earth’s history. Much of its landscape was shaped while it was part of Gondwana, and its famous Jurassic dolerite was emplaced around 175 million years ago. The later breakup of Gondwana and separation from Antarctica and mainland Australia helped create the island we know today.
We really appreciate this suggestion. A deeper geological chapter would have added another fascinating layer to the story, and we’ll keep that in mind for future videos. Thank you for watching and for adding such an interesting perspective.

comments.author: @GMN360
comments.text: My great, great grandmother was transported to Van Diemen’s  Land (now Tasmania)in 1842, aged 18.  Originally she was to be sent to the women’s prison factory in Hobart.  Because of overcrowding she and 79 other female convicts were shipped to Launceston.  When I young, it was  great shame to have convict heritage and much was done by the children to hide their parent’s history.  Fortunately that shame has changed and I am eternally grateful to the Female Convict Research Centre, the Tasmanian Government and Trove Australia and all other organisations for all they have done in preserving records, implementing a comprehensive website for research and holding an annual conference.  From the knowledge gained about my g.g. grandmother. I have been able to research her children and their descendants which has proved that she may have been transported but she and her husband (a Welshman and free settler) brought their children up to be responsible adults.  I now have a wealth of Launceston, Melbourne, Sydney and Perth family history.  I visited Hobart, again when much younger on a regular basis on business and had no idea of my ancestry.  How I would love to be able to visit Launceston and Hobart  now armed with all this knowledge. Also it would be a bonus to see the beautiful island again.

comments.author: @Pedro-y3u1e
comments.text: Quite a good story but failed to do justice to the incredible famous seafood and rural produce. Tasmania is also home to the now protected biggest freshwater lobster in the world capable of growing to over 5kg or 12 pounds. On the dark side were massacres and near elimination of the traditional owners and the misguided extinction of the amazing striped and pouched Tasmanian Tiger last recorded alive in the 1930s.

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text: Thank you for such a detailed and thoughtful comment. You’re right that Tasmania’s seafood, rural produce, and unique wildlife deserve much more attention, and the giant freshwater crayfish is a fascinating part of the island’s natural heritage. The darker chapters of Tasmania’s history, including the violence and dispossession suffered by Aboriginal Tasmanians and the extinction of the Thylacine, also deserve to be treated carefully and respectfully. We really appreciate you adding this perspective, and we’ll keep these points in mind for future videos.
